lesson.title: Making a neutral formula

lead.text: Positive and negative ions attract one another. Put a great many of them together and they pull into a regular, repeating block called a crystal, with every positive ion surrounded by negative ones and the other way round. A substance built like this is called an ionic compound.

An ionic compound has no overall charge, even though every ion inside it is charged. A lump with a net charge would pull on everything near it, and a spoonful of salt does nothing of the kind. So the ions in the crystal must come in numbers that make the charges add to zero.
The simplest case is sodium chloride. A sodium ion carries +1 and a chloride ion carries −1, so one of each cancels exactly and the crystal holds them in equal numbers.

diagram.alt: A flat slice of a sodium chloride crystal as a grid of circles. Sodium ions with a plus one charge and chloride ions with a minus one charge alternate in every row and column, so each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge.
diagram.caption: A small slice of the crystal. Positive and negative ions alternate, and there are as many of one as the other, so the charges cancel.

lead.text: Aim for a total charge of zero. A chloride ion carries −1 and a magnesium ion carries +2.

steps.headline: Writing the ratio as a formula

lead.text: A formula is a short way of writing down the hand you have chosen. Each kind of ion gets its symbol, and a small number written after it and lowered, the subscript, says how many of that ion the compound has. When there is just one of an ion the 1 is left out. The positive ion is written first.

Aluminium ions carry +3 and chloride ions carry −1, so it takes three chloride ions to cancel one aluminium ion. That hand is written AlCl₃: one aluminium ion and three chloride ions, with the 1 left out. In the picture the second case shows sodium chloride, NaCl, for comparison.

afterFigure.text: The formula records a ratio of ions and not a count. AlCl₃ says that for every aluminium ion in the crystal there are three chloride ions. The real crystal holds enormous numbers of each.

steps.headline: When the charges don't match one for one

lead.text: Matching +2 with two −1 ions is easy. It gets harder when neither charge is a simple multiple of the other, and the card game shows the way. Suppose one kind of card scores +4 and another scores −6. One of each leaves a total of −2, so we need more cards.

Think about the totals. Adding +4 cards gives totals of 4, 8, 12 and so on, and adding −6 cards gives 6, 12 and so on. The first total they share is 12, so the smallest winning hand is three of the +4 cards and two of the −6 cards, since 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 6 = 12.

Ions work the same way. Find the smallest total charge that both ion charges divide into, and divide it by each charge in turn. The two answers are the numbers of ions in the smallest hand, and they become the subscripts.

diagram.alt: Two piles of cards, one of plus four cards and one of minus six cards, each with a running total. One of each totals minus two, two of each totals minus four, and three plus four cards with two minus six cards total zero.
diagram.caption: Each pile has its own total. The totals cancel when three +4 cards meet two −6 cards. Use the buttons to step through the hands.

steps.headline: Na⁺ and S²⁻ form a compound. What is its formula?

workedSteps.text: Write the charges: +1 on each sodium ion, −2 on each sulfide ion.
One Na⁺ cancels only half of the −2, so you need two of them.
Write the counts as subscripts. A 1 is left out.

steps.headline: Aluminium oxide is built from Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Find the ratio.

workedSteps.text: Three O²⁻ ions bring a total charge of −6.
Find how many Al³⁺ ions bring +6.

lead.text: Find the smallest whole numbers of each ion whose charges cancel. Work out the shared total first.

steps.headline: One formula for a whole crystal

lead.text: A grain of salt holds a vast number of sodium ions and chloride ions in a regular pattern. No pair of ions is set apart, and none belongs to a separate little molecule. So a formula for an ionic compound describes the ratio of ions across the whole crystal and nothing smaller.

It also gives the simplest ratio that makes the charges cancel, and that smallest hand is called the formula unit. Two sodium ions with two chloride ions would cancel too, but Na₂Cl₂ describes the same crystal less simply, so we write NaCl.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both. The crystal is the same in either, and only the simplest ratio is written as the formula.

lead.text: Think about what a formula can say about a crystal that holds billions of ions.
Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻. Write the simplest formula unit and count the ions in it.

lesson.orientation: Find whole-number ion ratios that balance electric charge.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In a card game, every card carries a score. One card scores +6 and the others each score −2. A hand wins when its cards add up to zero, and the best hand is the smallest one that gets there. Put the +6 card down and you need three of the −2 cards to win. Two would leave the total at +2, and four would take it down to −2.

A pinch of table salt plays the same game. The last lesson ended with atoms that lose or gain electrons and become ions with charges such as +1 and −1. A grain of salt is a heap of such ions, and it carries no overall charge, which means the ions it holds must add up to zero just as a winning hand does.
This lesson plays that game with real ions. We choose the smallest hand of ions whose charges cancel, and then write the hand down as a formula.

diagram.alt: A card game. One card scoring plus six is shown beside two, three or four cards scoring minus two. Two minus-two cards leave a total of plus two, three give zero and four give minus two.
diagram.caption: The winning hand is the one that adds up to zero. Use the buttons to try two, three or four −2 cards with the +6 card.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the simplest neutral formula for an ionic compound from the charges on its ions.
intro.whyItMatters: A formula tells you how much of each ingredient a compound holds.

recap.keyIdea: An ionic compound is neutral, so its ions come in the smallest whole-number ratio whose charges add to zero. The formula writes that ratio and does not describe a separate molecule.

blocks.text: Back at the card table, you balanced +2 against two −1 ions and Na⁺ against S²⁻. You also found that Ca²⁺ with N³⁻ takes three calcium ions to two nitride ions, and each time the charges added to zero.

recap.nextHook: Not every pair of atoms hands electrons over. The next lesson looks at atoms that share electrons in pairs, and at how the sharing holds them together.

questions.prompt: How many Cl⁻ ions balance one Mg²⁺ ion?
hints: Make the total charge zero.
Read the positive ion's charge before counting negative ions.
How many single negative charges cancel the magnesium charge?
questions.onCorrect: 2. Each chloride is −1, so two cancel magnesium's +2.

misconceptions.feedback: One chloride cancels only half of magnesium's positive charge.

questions.prompt: In Al₂O₃, how many Al³⁺ ions accompany three O²⁻ ions?
hints: Find the positive count needed to reach +6.
Three oxide ions contribute −6 altogether.
Divide the required positive charge 6 by 3 per aluminium ion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three oxide ions total −6; two aluminium ions total +6.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Two +3 ions give +6, which cancels the −6 from three oxide ions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of oxide ions, which the question gives. Find the aluminium count.
That is the charge to cancel, not the number of ions.

questions.prompt: What does NaCl describe in a sodium chloride crystal?
hints: Think about what a lattice of ions has in place of separate molecules.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: NaCl records the simplest ratio of sodium and chloride ions in a lattice.

choices.label: Two neutral atoms with no attraction

questions.onCorrect: A formula unit gives the ratio of ions in the crystal. It does not describe a separate molecule.

misconceptions.feedback: A sodium chloride crystal has no separate two-atom molecules. It is a lattice of ions.
The ions attract strongly, and they are not neutral atoms.

questions.prompt: In the simplest formula MgO, how many oxide ions accompany one magnesium ion?
hints: Compare the sizes of the opposite charges.
One magnesium and one oxide have equal and opposite charges.
Use the smallest positive whole-number count that cancels +2.
questions.onCorrect: 1. The charges are equal and opposite, so one of each ion is the simplest ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: Two oxide ions would bring −4, which is more than magnesium's charge needs.

questions.prompt: Calcium forms Ca²⁺. How many Cl⁻ ions are needed per calcium ion?
hints: Balance charge using whole ions.
Each chloride cancels one unit of positive charge.
How many single negative charges cancel the calcium charge?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two chloride ions supply a total of −2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each chloride cancels one unit of charge, so calcium's +2 needs two.

misconceptions.feedback: One chloride cancels only one of calcium's two positive charges.

questions.prompt: Why does aluminium oxide use the ratio Al₂O₃?
hints: Count net charge rather than guessed neighbours.

acceptedIdeas: It makes the total charge zero

choices.label: It makes the total charge zero
Every ion must have three neighbours
Oxygen changes to a positive ion

questions.onCorrect: The ratio is chosen so that the total charge is zero: two +3 ions cancel three −2 ions.

misconceptions.feedback: Ions are not counted by neighbours. The ratio comes from the charges.
Oxygen forms a negative ion. The ratio balances the charges.

questions.prompt: How many −2 cards make a winning hand with one +6 card?
hints: The total must be zero. How much negative score do you need?
Each −2 card supplies a fixed amount of that.
Divide the score you need to cancel by the score of one card.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The −2 cards must total −6, and 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cards.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The positive and negative scores have to cancel. Ions in a compound are balanced in just the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the score to cancel, not the number of cards.
Two −2 cards total −4, which is not enough.

questions.prompt: Why is the formula Na₂S rather than NaS?

acceptedIdeas: One Na⁺ only cancels half of the sulfide ion's charge

choices.label: One Na⁺ only cancels half of the sulfide ion's charge
Sulfur always has a subscript of 1
Sodium atoms are smaller than sulfur atoms

questions.onCorrect: Right: the subscripts are chosen so that the charges add to zero.

misconceptions.feedback: The subscript on S is 1 because one sulfide ion is enough. The count of Na⁺ comes from the charge.
Size does not set the ratio. Charge does.

questions.prompt: Ca²⁺ and N³⁻ form a neutral compound. What is the smallest number of Ca²⁺ ions in the simplest formula?
hints: Find the smallest total charge that both +2 and −3 divide into.
That total is the same size on both sides.
Divide it by the charge on one calcium ion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three Ca²⁺ give +6 and two N³⁻ give −6, so 3 calcium ions.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Three Ca²⁺ (+6) balance two N³⁻ (−6), the smallest whole-number match.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of nitride ions. The question asks about calcium.
That is the charge to balance, not the number of ions.

questions.prompt: Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ form Fe₂O₃. How many ions are in one formula unit altogether?
hints: Read the two subscripts.
A subscript counts the ions of that kind.
Add the two counts.
questions.onCorrect: 5. The subscripts count the ions of each kind, so add them.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the subscripts. Add them to count the ions.
That is only the iron ions. Count the oxide ions as well.
